summary: Defines MIME Object Security Services, a protocol that uses the multipart/signed and multipart/encrypted framework to add digital signatures and encryption to MIME objects. It was standards-track but is now historic.

eli5.summary: A method for signing and locking email so only the right person can read it and everyone can check who sent it.

questions: what is mime object security services
how does moss differ from pem
how does moss sign an email
subtitle: Signing and encrypting MIME email with plain public key pairs, no certificates required.

tldr.problem: MIME had no security services, and the older PEM scheme only handled text messages and required every user to have a certificate.
tldr.mechanism: MOSS fills the multipart/signed and multipart/encrypted frameworks with control headers (Originator-ID, MIC-Info, DEK-Info, Recipient-ID, Key-Info) that carry a digital signature or an encrypted data key.
tldr.outcome: It was a Standards Track specification and is now Historic. It protects any MIME object, and users only need a public/private key pair.

today: RFC 1848 is Historic and the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes it. Its frame, RFC 1847, defines the multipart/signed and multipart/encrypted types that MOSS fills in.

sections.title: Introduction and Goals
sections.content:
MIME Object Security Services (MOSS) applies digital signature and encryption services to MIME objects, using end-to-end cryptography at the application layer between an originator and a recipient. Public key cryptography supports signatures and key management, and symmetric cryptography supports the encryption itself.

MOSS is based in large part on RFC 1421, the PEM protocol. PEM only covered text messages. MOSS uses the multipart/signed and multipart/encrypted framework of RFC 1847 instead, so any single or multi-part MIME object can be protected. A user only needs one public/private key pair. The private key must not be disclosed, and the public key must reach the people the user wants to talk to securely.
sections.eli5: MOSS lets you sign or lock any kind of email, not just plain text. All you need is a pair of keys: one you keep secret and one you share.

sections.title: Signing a Message
sections.content:
To sign, the body part is first canonicalized. It is converted to 7bit (using quoted-printable or base64 for any 8bit or binary content), and its line delimiters are converted to <CR><LF>. The line delimiter conversion is used only to compute the signature. The data itself is sent without it, because SMTP servers may change line delimiters in transit.

The signature is made by hashing the data and encrypting the hash with the originator's private key. The control information is a set of one-line headers: one Version: 5 header first, then at least one pair of Originator-ID: and MIC-Info:. MIC-Info: carries the hash algorithm, the signature algorithm and the signature value. Both parts go into a multipart/signed object whose protocol is application/moss-signature, and whose micalg parameter repeats the hash algorithm.

To verify, the recipient recomputes the hash over the prepared data, decrypts the hash in the control information with the originator's public key, and compares them. Matching hashes show only that the data is what was signed. Knowing who signed also requires that the binding between the owner's name and the public key was checked beforehand.
sections.eli5: You write a short fingerprint of your message and seal it with your secret stamp. Anyone with your public stamp-checker can see the message was not changed and that you made it.

sections.title: Encrypting a Message
sections.content:
To encrypt, the originator makes a data encrypting key, encrypts the data with it, and then encrypts that key with each recipient's public key. The control information has one Version: header, one DEK-Info: header naming the algorithm and mode (with parameters such as an initialization vector), and one Recipient-ID: and Key-Info: pair for each recipient.

This is packed in a multipart/encrypted object with protocol="application/moss-keys". The first part is the key information and the second part is the encrypted data, labeled application/octet-stream. Implementors are told to always add a pair for the originator too, so that an undelivered message can still be read by its sender.

To decrypt, the recipient looks for a Recipient-ID: that identifies them, uses their private key to open the following Key-Info:, and then decrypts the data. The result is a MIME body part ready for a MIME agent.
sections.eli5: You lock the message with one random key, then put a copy of that key into a tiny lockbox for each friend, each opened only by that friend's own key.

sections.title: Identifying People and Keys
sections.content:
Unlike PEM, MOSS does not require certificates. The Originator-ID: and Recipient-ID: headers carry an identifier, which is a name form plus a key selector that makes one key unique for that name. Three name forms are defined: RFC 822 email addresses, arbitrary strings, and X.500 distinguished names (kept for PEM compatibility).

There are five identifier types: email address (EN), arbitrary string (STR), distinguished name (DN), the public key itself (PK, optionally with a name-form subset), and issuer name plus serial number (IS). Using the public key alone also allows anonymous but recognizable encrypted mail, because recipients know repeated messages come from the same key. A recipient of a PK identifier must check that the claimed name-to-key association is real.
sections.eli5: Each key gets a name tag, such as an email address, plus a number so you can tell your keys apart.

sections.title: Key Management Content Types
sections.content:
Two content types let users ask for and send key material. application/mosskey-request asks for a public key or certificate chain (Subject:), a certificate revocation list chain (Issuer:), or certification of a self-signed certificate (Certification:). application/mosskey-data returns public keys, certificate chains or CRL chains.

The RFC states plainly that it makes no provision for checking that conveyed keys are authentic: an interloper could swap the public key or identifier. Recipients must verify the data before use, for example through certificates or because the responder signed the reply.
sections.eli5: You can mail a note asking, "please send me your public key." The reply comes in another note, but you still have to make sure nobody swapped it on the way.

sections.title: How MOSS Differs from PEM
sections.content:
Section 8 lists the differences. MOSS users need only a key pair rather than certificates, and MOSS allows more name forms. Its messages are no longer limited to ASCII text, and signing and encryption can be applied separately and in any order, whereas PEM only encrypted signed bodies. Transfer encoding, the Proc-Type: header and the Content-Domain: header are handled by MIME instead. MOSS explicitly excludes symmetric key management and requires signed data to be in 7bit form.

The RFC also notes that separating the two services allows different key pairs for each. A company could then hold the decryption key of an employee for emergencies without being able to sign as that employee. Its security section reads, in full, that the entire document is about security.
sections.eli5: MOSS is a more flexible cousin of PEM. You can sign, lock, or do both, and it works on pictures and sounds as well as words.

data.title: multipart/signed with MOSS
data.code:
Content-Type: multipart/signed;
  protocol="application/moss-signature";
  micalg="rsa-md5"; boundary="Signed Message"

--Signed Message
Content-Type: text/plain

This is some example text.
--Signed Message
Content-Type: application/moss-signature

Version: 5
Originator-ID: ID-INFORMATION
MIC-Info: RSA-MD5,RSA,SIGNATURE-INFORMATION
--Signed Message--

data.title: multipart/encrypted with MOSS
data.code:
Content-Type: multipart/encrypted;
  protocol="application/moss-keys";
  boundary="Encrypted Message"

--Encrypted Message
Content-Type: application/moss-keys

Version: 5
DEK-Info: DES-CBC,DEK-INFORMATION
Recipient-ID: ID-INFORMATION
Key-Info: RSA,KEY-INFORMATION
--Encrypted Message
Content-Type: application/octet-stream

ENCRYPTED-DATA
--Encrypted Message--
